name: Black Hole
text:
The Dzhanibekov Effect: The Mind-Bending Flip of Rotating Objects in Space This counterintuitive phenomenon—where a freely rotating rigid body suddenly flips its orientation 180° periodically without any external torque—perfectly illustrates the Intermediate Axis Theorem (also called the Tennis Racket Theorem).For any object with three distinct principal moments of inertia (I₁ < I₂ < I₃):Rotation about the axes with the maximum (I₃) and minimum (I₁) moments is stable.
Rotation about the intermediate axis (I₂) is unstable: even tiny perturbations cause the object to tumble and flip dramatically.

This arises from the nonlinear nature of Euler's equations for torque-free rigid body motion. The instability grows exponentially around the intermediate axis, leading to periodic reversals.The effect was dramatically noticed in 1985 by Soviet cosmonaut Vladimir Dzhanibekov while spinning a wing nut in microgravity aboard the Salyut 7 space station—it unexpectedly flipped!On Earth, air resistance and gravity mask it, but you can glimpse it by tossing a tennis racket or book while spinning it around its intermediate http://axis.In space, it's crystal clear. Recent demos include Chinese astronauts, NASA experiments, and as of 2025, astronaut Don Pettit on the ISS spinning a camera to showcase the effect during his http://mission.It's a reminder of how classical mechanics can still surprise us—no quantum weirdness needed! Pure rotational dynamics in action.  #DzhanibekovEffect
